title: DNS Systems Engineering: Infrastructure Triage
subject: DNS
description: In a modern enterprise, 'The Network is Down' is almost always a DNS failure. In this activity, you will step into the role of a Systems Administrator managing a complex Windows Server environment. You'll move past simple 'pings' to analyze SRV records, recursion logic, and Active Directory replication health to restore critical services.
reportOverview: This report summarizes your diagnostic accuracy across enterprise DNS scenarios. Use it to identify gaps in your understanding of name resolution hierarchy and zone synchronization.
evidenceInstructions:
Instructions:
1) Analyze the symptom and examine the provided artifacts (nslookup, ipconfig, event logs).
2) Choose the Triage step that provides the most actionable data.
3) Identify the Diagnosis based on the technical evidence.
4) Select the professional remediation (Fix) that aligns with best practices.
5) Document your change note for the ticketing system.

tickets.title: Workstation: 'The specified domain could not be contacted'
tickets.summary: A workstation in the Accounting department cannot join the domain. It has full internet access, but the NetSetup log indicates a failure to locate the Domain Controller.
validations: Confirm client is using internal DNS (DCs).
Confirm SRV lookup resolves after change.

debrief.summary: Active Directory is entirely dependent on Service (SRV) records to locate resources. By using public resolvers (8.8.8.8), the workstation was asking the internet for internal LDAP records that don't exist in the public namespace.
debrief.takeaway: Domain joins are DNS-dependent: point clients to internal DC DNS to ensure AD-specific SRV records can be discovered.

triage.q: The client has internet access but cannot find the domain. What is the first configuration you must examine on the client?
options: Check the 'Domain Admins' group membership
Verify the assigned DNS servers in the IPv4 properties to ensure they point to local Domain Controllers
Disable the Windows Firewall to see if LDAP traffic is being filtered
Check if the Netlogon service is running on the local workstation

diagnosis.q: The nslookup shows NXDOMAIN for the _msdcs record, and ipconfig shows Google DNS. Why is the join failing?
options: The Domain Controller is offline
Public DNS servers (8.8.8.8) are not authoritative for the internal AD namespace and cannot resolve SRV records
The workstation is on a different VLAN than the Domain Controller
The workstation's clock is out of sync with the DC by more than 5 minutes

fix.q: What is the most professional way to remediate this across the department?
options: Manually add the DC's IP to the 'hosts' file on every machine
Configure DHCP Scope Option 006 to provide the IP addresses of the internal DNS servers to all clients
Set the DNS servers to 'Obtain Automatically' and hope for the best
Run 'ipconfig /registerdns' on the workstation

tickets.title: Global External Resolution Failure
tickets.summary: Internal resources (File shares, Intranet) are working perfectly, but no users in the company can access external websites or resolve public hostnames.
validations: Confirm external nslookup succeeds after change.
Check DNS event logs for timeouts.

debrief.summary: In many locked-down enterprise environments, root hints are blocked by firewalls to prevent unauthorized DNS traffic. Configuring explicit Forwarders to a trusted resolver (like an ISP or public DNS) is the standard way to bridge internal and external resolution.
debrief.takeaway: When internal works but external fails, recursion is likely broken. Check Forwarders and verify that the firewall allows Port 53 outbound from the DNS server.

triage.q: Users can reach internal sites but not external. What is the primary setting to check on the internal DNS server to see how it handles unknown queries?
options: The 'Forwarders' tab in the DNS Server properties
The 'Reverse Lookup Zones' for external IP ranges
The 'Scavenging' settings for stale records
The 'Trust Anchors' for DNSSEC validation

diagnosis.q: The Forwarders list is empty. Why is the server not successfully using its Root Hints to resolve external names?
options: Root Hints only work for .com domains
The corporate firewall is likely blocking outbound UDP 53 from the DC to the internet root servers
The server's NIC is set to 'Public' profile
The DNS server is not authorized in Active Directory

fix.q: What is the recommended fix to restore external resolution safely?
options: Configure the DNS server to forward queries to a reliable upstream resolver (e.g., 9.9.9.9 or 1.1.1.1)
Delete the internal zone and allow the server to become a caching-only server
Direct users to use 8.8.8.8 as their secondary DNS on their local machines
Disable the 'Recursion' property on the DNS server

tickets.title: Site-to-Site Record Inconsistency
tickets.summary: An A-record for a new server was created at the HQ office (DC-01). Two hours later, users at the Branch office (DC-02) still cannot resolve the name.
artifact: Last attempt @ [Time] failed, result 1722 (The RPC server is unavailable)
validations: Confirm replication is healthy after remediation.
Confirm DNS record appears on DC2.
Validate SRV and host records are consistent.

debrief.summary: AD-Integrated DNS zones store their data inside the Active Directory database. If the underlying AD replication is failing (due to network, RPC, or Kerberos issues), the DNS records will never reach the other Domain Controllers.
debrief.takeaway: DNS data is only as fresh as your AD replication. Use 'repadmin' to diagnose sync issues before troubleshooting the DNS service itself.

triage.q: Records are inconsistent across servers. What command-line tool provides the best insight into the health of the data transport between these servers?
options: nslookup -type=all
repadmin /showrepl
dcdiag /test:dns
ipconfig /flushdns

diagnosis.q: Repadmin reports an RPC failure (1722). What does this imply about the DNS inconsistency?
options: The DNS zone is set to 'Primary' on one and 'Secondary' on the other
An underlying network or service failure is preventing Active Directory (and thus DNS) from synchronizing
The record's TTL is too high
The Branch office DNS server is out of disk space

fix.q: What is the correct troubleshooting path?
options: Manually recreate the record on DC-02 to bypass the error
Resolve the RPC/connectivity issues between DCs to restore AD replication, which will automatically sync the DNS records
Convert the zone to a Secondary zone on DC-02
Reboot DC-01 to force a push of the DNS database
